analysis.one_liner: Halts large food and agriculture mergers for 18 months while a commission studies market concentration.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2018 with no cosponsors, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would freeze mergers among the biggest agribusiness, food and beverage manufacturing, and grocery retail companies for up to 18 months, with an exception the Attorney General could grant for a company in financial distress. It would also create a commission to study how much a few large firms now control meatpacking, seeds, grain, and grocery sales, and recommend changes to antitrust law. The stated aim is to restore competition so family farmers get better prices for what they sell and shoppers do not pay a widening markup at the store.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers who would face more buyers competing for their cattle, hogs, grain, and milk; small and mid-sized food processors and independent grocers who would face less consolidated rivals; rural communities whose economies depend on viable family farms; and shoppers, since the bill targets the gap between low farm prices and high supermarket prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Family farmers, rural towns, food shoppers

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings note the top 4 beef packers grew from 32% to 85% of the market and the top 4 pork packers from 36% to 71%, leaving farmers few buyers for their animals; a merger freeze would stop that consolidation from getting worse while the study commission completes its work [S3].

The findings state farmers now receive about 15 cents of every retail food dollar, down from 41 cents in 1950, while net farm income has fallen by more than half since 2013; the commission is directed to study why low farm prices have not produced lower supermarket prices [S3].

The commission would include members currently engaged in farming or ranching and would hold hearings in four different agriculture regions, not just Washington, and report recommendations for changing antitrust laws to keep the farm marketplace competitive [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large agribusiness companies, meatpackers, seed and chemical firms, big food and beverage manufacturers, and large grocery chains that would have to wait out the moratorium before merging or acquiring rivals, plus their shareholders who would forgo some deal-making during that window.

drawbacks.text: A blanket freeze on large mergers for 18 months could block deals that would actually help efficiency or rescue a struggling company; the bill allows the Attorney General to waive it only in extraordinary circumstances like insolvency, which critics could call too rigid [S3].

The bill exempts agricultural cooperatives from its definitions, so farmer-owned co-ops are treated differently from other buyers, and transactions valued under the bill's size thresholds ($160 million in sales or assets on one side) are untouched, meaning some large deals could still proceed [S3].
The bill itself changes no antitrust rules; it delays mergers and produces a study with recommendations, so its benefits depend on Congress acting later on whatever the commission proposes [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is real but bounded: an 18-month pause on new consolidation in markets where four firms already control 70-85% of meatpacking, plus a serious study directed at why shoppers' costs and farmers' incomes have moved in opposite directions. The main costs fall on large food and agribusiness firms that would forgo mergers during the freeze, and the risk is that a temporary moratorium plus a commission is a modest tool against decades of consolidation — it does not itself restore competition. On balance it was designed to slow a trend harming farmers and rural communities at comparatively small cost to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on August 28, 2018, near the end of the 115th Congress [S1][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary; no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with zero cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large agribusiness, meatpacking, seed and grocery companies, which faced no merger moratorium and no commission studying their market power, because the bill never advanced; the mergers it would have frozen were free to proceed as before.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey (bill sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Food and Agribusiness Merger Moratorium and Antitrust Review Act of 2018 and delivered introductory remarks when it was read into the record.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley)
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on August 28, 2018 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and its only sponsor was a Democrat with no cosponsors of either party, so the record shows no measurable partisan split on the merits.

industries.note: The bill would have blocked mergers among the largest processors and dealers for 18 months, directly limiting further consolidation of markets where the top 4 beef packers already hold 85% and top 4 pork packers 71% of sales. Fewer dominant buyers means farmers could get better prices for livestock and grain [S3].

Classified as agricultural input suppliers, they would have been covered by the merger moratorium; the bill's findings note three firms now control roughly two-thirds of the world's commodity crop seeds and about 70% of farm chemicals, and corn seed costs have nearly quadrupled in 20 years. Competition among seed suppliers would have worked in farmers' favor [S3].

industries.industry: Large grocery retail and food and beverage manufacturing chains
industries.note: Retailers and processors above the bill's size thresholds would have been barred from acquiring large rivals during the moratorium. The bill targets the widening gap between what shoppers pay and what farmers receive, implying some of that margin is captured by concentrated processing and retail firms [S3].

The bill's stated purpose is to increase farmers' bargaining power and economic prospects by reversing concentration; it excludes agricultural cooperatives from its restrictions, so farmer-owned businesses would not be restrained by the moratorium [S3].
